why.say: Let me put two numbers on the board. John Doe's Specials alone come to $16,401.40. Robert Smith carries $10,000 with Keystone. So what makes Keystone pay all of it, inside 30 days? Hold that thought, because the answer is a Time-Limited Demand for the limits, and it forces Keystone to decide on the record. Here's the catch, though. If the demand is vague, over limits, thin or unproven, a refusal costs Keystone nothing. If it's clear, reasonable, within limits, documented and timed, an unreasonable refusal can matter. That's five elements, and we're going to reveal them one at a time today.
why.ask: What makes Keystone pay all $10,000 of it, inside 30 days?

map.say: Before the mechanics, here's the road for the Time-Limited Demand. First, confirm the foundation: the statute of limitations, liability and coverage, each from its document. Second, a demand within limits, with clear terms: $10,000, who and what is released, and how to accept. Third, a reasonable window, with conditions Keystone can actually meet, and thirty days. Fourth, a package complete enough to evaluate inside that window. And fifth, service by certified mail and email, with the deadline docketed from receipt. Atty. Thorne decides every term; you make sure each step is done and proven.

theory.say: Before we get to the five elements, I want you to hear this: a demand isn't a request for money. It's the presentation of a debt owed. And it stands on three pillars, the statute of limitations, the liability framework and the coverage analysis. Know why the paperwork exists and you'll build it right. The Time-Limited Demand is a within-limits demand with a stated window, which forces a decision on the record. Then there's the Why Factor: every bill carries the reason the treatment was necessary, so the adjuster evaluates a documented recovery, not a pile of invoices. And before anything goes out, we do the Final Scrub for the usual adjuster traps, like billing overlaps, an unexplained pre-existing condition or an unverified balance.
theory.ask: Which of these four have you run into before, and where would it turn up on John Doe's file?

frame.say: Three best practices sit under every demand we send. First, the 30-Day Rule. Once the client reaches MMI, the demand targets MMI plus 30 days. John Doe reached MMI on 06/12/2026, so the target was 07/12/2026. Any later date belongs to Atty. Thorne, with his reason recorded, and ours went out on 07/20/2026. Second, photo impact. We lead with the most graphic image on file, Property Damage or injury, because it sets the tone before the adjuster reads a word. Third, the Why Factor again: every bill in the demand carries why that treatment was necessary for his recovery.
frame.ask: Where is John Doe against the 30-Day Rule, and whose call was the 07/20/2026 service date?

rules.say: Here are the rules, and where your role stops. Confirm the foundation first: the SOL docketed for 02/06/2028, liability from Smith's stop-sign citation, Ruth Calloway and the doorbell video, and coverage from Keystone's Dec Page showing $10,000 BI. The demand is for exactly that $10,000. Every term has to be acceptable as written: Smith and Keystone released, for the BI claim only, plus Smith's affidavit of no other insurance. Ask only what Keystone can deliver in 30 days, with the Big Four complete. The letter names what starts the clock, delivery of the certified mailing, and we serve certified with return receipt and by email. The gap goes on page one, and causation leads with the 03/13/2026 MRI. Bad faith is a legal conclusion, and it's Atty. Thorne's. You build, audit, serve and prove delivery. You never set terms, grant extensions or value the claim.
rules.ask: The email reached Dana Whitfield on 07/20 and the certified mail on 07/22. When does the window close, and how would Keystone know?

model.say: This is John Doe's demand, with the five elements pinned to it. Badge one is the $10,000 amount, within limits. Two is the release and affidavit terms, which are clear. Three is the conditions and the 30 days to meet them, so it's reasonable. Four is the enclosure list, documented. Five is the deadline and delivery lines, timed. Now look at the clock bar on the right: served 07/20/2026, received 07/22/2026 on the return receipt, and the window closes 08/21/2026. That's your answer from a minute ago, and Keystone knows it because the letter says the clock runs from delivery of the certified mailing. Notice the red warning up top, too: an ambiguous term is an escape hatch. Each badge is a door Keystone could refuse through, and this demand shuts all five.
model.ask: Which of the five doors do you think Keystone would try first if we'd left it open?

job.say: Let's follow this through on the job. It starts when MMI is declared on 06/12/2026. You docket MMI plus 30 and open the Demand Package task in CMS. That lands on 07/12/2026, a Sunday, and since it's an internal target, we work it early, on Friday 07/10. Legal deadlines counted forward roll to the next business day instead, and a later service date gets recorded as Atty. Thorne's, with his reason. When he approves the terms, you record them exactly in Case Notes before you draft a word. When the return receipt shows delivery on 07/22/2026, you docket 08/21/2026 from that receipt date, with reminders. And if Keystone writes or calls before the deadline, you log it word for word and route it to Atty. Thorne the same day. You change nothing on terms or time.

dodont.say: Now for a game I call Three Clues, One Rule. I'll reveal three clues about something a Case Manager did on this demand. You call it, Do or Don't, and then you name the rule behind it. Here's what's in play. Docketing from the return receipt date, never the mailing date. Leading with the value-drivers: the MRI herniation, the injection, the residual right-arm paresthesia at MMI, clear liability. Remembering the window is for acceptance, not payment. And the traps: a demand with no stated deadline, a timeline that leaves the gap out, a demand sent before MMI. One more thing. If I hear anybody call this a bad-faith letter, I'm stopping you. It's a Time-Limited Demand, and whether a refusal is bad faith is Atty. Thorne's legal conclusion.
dodont.ask: What makes a gap explanation hold up with an adjuster, and who supplies it?

why.say: I want to start with the net, not the gross, because BI alone leaves John Doe nothing. Take Keystone's $10,000, pull out the fee and costs, and you're at $6,179.92. His unreduced liens are $6,485.00. Do the subtraction and he walks away empty-handed. That's why the UM layers matter so much: they change his net. And here's the uncomfortable part. A technicality can lose them. A release signed too early. A consent nobody obtained. A UM demand sent before BI is exhausted. Any one of those puts a hole in his safety net. This lesson is about locking those escape hatches before Host UM and Relative UM open.
why.ask: If BI on its own leaves him nothing, what are the UM layers worth to John Doe?

theory.say: Think of UM as the client's financial safety net. Once the at-fault policy is exhausted, first-party coverage makes up the difference, up to its limits. Four ideas hold it together. First, the net check: John Doe doesn't care about the gross, only what's left after fees and unreduced liens. Second, BI exhaustion: the at-fault carrier pays its full limit, and that pulls the contract trigger, so the UM claim becomes a second phase. Third, consent and subrogation waiver: the UM carrier consents and waives subrogation, or substitutes its own check, so the UM claim survives the BI release. And fourth, front-load the proof. The at-fault Dec Page, the signed release and the consents go up front, which strips away the technicality defense on page one.
theory.ask: Have you seen a consent-to-settle request on a file before, and what happened when it was missing?

theory2.say: Let's keep going, because a UM claim is a different animal. The UM carrier insures our client, so the claim shifts from third-party to first-party. It's a contract claim, and it's still adversarial. Don't forget that part. UM also doesn't simply pay its limit. It pays the gap between damages and what's already been collected. Then you need to know the policy's form. An offset policy subtracts the BI from its UM limit, while add-on or stacked coverage pays on top. And Relative UM sits as excess. It answers only above the primary layers, so the gap it pays starts right where BI and Host UM end.
theory2.ask: If Harbor Point were an offset policy, how much room would be left on its $20,000 after Keystone's $10,000?

frame.say: Here's how the UM settlement actually gets calculated. Start with total case value, Medical Bills plus pain and suffering, as Atty. Thorne values them. That number is his, not ours. Subtract the BI settlement, the at-fault driver's maximum limit, which here is Keystone's full $10,000. What's left is the gap, and Harbor Point's Host UM covers it up to $20,000. Then comes Relative UM, as excess. Cardinal State answers only above BI and Host UM, so it picks up the gap above $30,000, up to its $10,000 limit. Stack it up and you can see how this file reaches $40,000, but only if the damages are proven above each layer.
frame.ask: Where does John Doe sit on this ladder right now, and which layer is still waiting to open?

rules.say: These are the rules, and here's where you stop. BI exhaustion comes first: Host UM opens once Keystone's $10,000 tender of 08/12/2026 is documented. Prove Keystone is all there is with its Dec Page and Smith's 08/10/2026 affidavit of no other insurance. The day after the tender, 08/13, the 30-Day Letters go to Harbor Point and Cardinal State asking each to consent and waive subrogation, or substitute its own check. Nothing goes to John Doe for signature until both consents are in writing, 08/24 and 08/26, and Atty. Thorne approves the release. Limit that release to Robert Smith, Keystone and the BI claim. Harbor Point confirmed add-on in writing on 03/02/2026; get the same in writing from Cardinal State. You prepare, track, catch and draft. You never interpret a policy or release for John Doe, or tell him to sign.
rules.ask: Keystone's draft release is in your inbox and Dana Whitfield wants it back today. What's wrong with it?

model.say: Picture this as a train line with six stations. One, the tender on 08/12. Two, the consent requests on 08/13. Three, the consents themselves, 08/24 and 08/26. Then comes that heavy orange gate: no release before both consents. Only after it do we reach four, the Limited Release on 08/28. Five, the UM demands on 08/31. Six, Keystone's check on 09/04. Above the rail is the ladder we're protecting: BI $10,000, Host UM $20,000 as add-on, Relative UM $10,000 as excess. And down in the corner, struck through, is the line from Keystone's 08/14 draft, “all other persons, firms, corporations and insurers.” That's the word you just went hunting for. The lesson of this slide is simple. Sequence is protection.
model.ask: What would have happened to the stack if station four had come before station three?

job.say: Now let's see how that runs at your desk. Keystone tenders the $10,000 on 08/12/2026. That's your trigger to prepare the 30-Day Letters, the consent-to-settle requests, to both UM carriers for Atty. Thorne's signature, using the template in the Action Plan Editor, and to docket each window. Both go out 08/13 with the tender, the Dec Page and the affidavit. On 08/14, Keystone's draft release arrives. You compare who and what it releases against the approved terms, and you flag the overbreadth. That “all other insurers” language goes to Atty. Thorne as an escalated task, and nothing goes to John Doe to sign. Once both consents are in writing and the Limited Release is signed on 08/28, you open two tracked CMS tasks for the UM demands, each with its carrier, claim number and adjuster.

dodont.say: Time for Three Clues, One Rule. I'll reveal three clues, you call Do or Don't, and then you name the rule. The rules in play: exhaustion proof goes at the front of each UM package. The source of the add-on confirmation, Harbor Point's 03/02/2026 letter, goes on the Coverage Matrix. Cardinal State's form gets confirmed in writing too, so no anti-stacking clause caps John Doe at $20,000. And the traps: treating Harbor Point and Cardinal State as friendly, letting an “all other insurers” release reach the client, promising full limits early, celebrating $40,000 before the liens are reduced. One warning before we play. Consent isn't a courtesy. It protects the UM carrier's subrogation right, which is exactly why releasing Smith without it can cost the coverage.
dodont.ask: John Doe is their insured, so why are Harbor Point and Cardinal State now adversaries?

case.say: Here's what just landed on the file. It's Monday, 07/20/2026, and Atty. Thorne writes that the Keystone BI demand gets a final audit and goes out today. The terms are approved for Dana Whitfield at Keystone Mutual, claim KM-26-440871: the $10,000 limits, a Limited Release of Robert Smith and Keystone only, Smith's affidavit of no other insurance, and 30 days from receipt. MMI was 06/12/2026, Dr. Reyes's Causation Letter and the Gap Explanation Record are on file, and the pre-demand audit put the Specials at $16,401.40. I'm handing you the demand specialist's draft. Fair warning, it has problems. Audit it against the Big Four and the Final Scrub, log every deficiency as a task, and bring it back for his signature. Nobody mails anything until the audit is logged.
case.ask: Before you open the draft, what are the first three things you'll check?

task.say: Here's your job. Audit the draft against the Big Four and the Final Scrub in the Action Plan Editor, and log each deficiency as an assigned CMS task rather than fixing it quietly. Assemble the package with the gap answered on page one of the timeline. Once Atty. Thorne signs, serve Keystone by certified mail with return receipt and by email through the Email Workspace, and log both. When the return receipt comes back dated 07/22/2026, docket the acceptance deadline from it, with reminders. Then you'll take a live call from Dana Whitfield. Confirm receipt and the 08/21/2026 deadline as written, agree to no extension, log her requests in her exact words, and send nothing without approval. You'll hand in an audited, served demand with proof of delivery and 08/21/2026 docketed.
task.ask: Suppose Dana Whitfield emails on day 25 asking for two more weeks. Who answers?

check.say: Before you log anything, check yourself. Is the amount $10,000, Keystone's BI limit per its 03/20/2026 Dec Page? Do the terms match Atty. Thorne's approval word for word? Are the Big Four complete, with Specials of $16,401.40 and the Riverton Drug receipts counted once? Did your Final Scrub catch the 05/04/2026 duplicate, taking Riverton Spine & Rehab from $6,290.00 to $6,105.00? Is the gap answered on page one, and are the 2021 low-back visits disclosed as resolved, with no neck history? Disclosed and distinguished, never hidden. Every deficiency should be a dated, assigned task, it should be served 07/20 both ways, and 08/21/2026 docketed from the 07/22 receipt. If you counted from the mailing date, you had the right idea and the wrong day. Any extension request goes to Atty. Thorne the same day.
check.ask: If you docketed from the mailing date, what day did you land on, and why is it wrong?

audit.say: Here's the enclosure set as the demand specialist built it, and here's your job: call every item. Keep it, replace it, pull it, add what's missing, or flag it for Atty. Thorne. Some of these are small and some of them cost John Doe real money. Exhibit E carries Riverton Spine and Rehab at six thousand two hundred and ninety dollars with the fourth of May billed twice, and Crescent's statement bills him fifteen hundred and forty dollars that an in-network provider can't bill him at all. Two things are missing that the letter leans on. When you hand it in you'll see the package as Atty. Thorne actually signed and served it on the twentieth of July, and you can mark your own audit against it.
audit.ask: Which item in this set would you least want Dana Whitfield to find first?

case.say: Look at the date first. It's Monday, 08/31/2026, and Keystone's check isn't here. Here's what landed from Atty. Thorne. BI is done: Keystone tendered $10,000 on 08/12 after Smith's affidavit of 08/10. Harbor Point consented on 08/24, Cardinal State on 08/26, and the Limited Release of Robert Smith and Keystone was signed 08/28. He wants the Host UM demand to Harbor Point for $20,000 and the Relative UM demand to Cardinal State for $10,000, as excess, with exhaustion on page one of each and the response deadline left blank for him. And remember, on 08/05 Keystone leaned on the 14-day gap and called the MRI degenerative. Expect the UM carriers to try the very same thing.
case.ask: With no check in hand today, what proves exhaustion?

task.say: You're not starting from a blank page. The audit closed on 07/15, and Atty. Thorne assigned the UM demands to the Demand Desk; their drafts are in the file. Your job is QC. Host UM goes to Marcus Bell at Harbor Point, HP-26-7741, for the $20,000 limit; Relative UM goes to Teresa Okafor at Cardinal State, CS-26-20355, for $10,000 as excess over Host UM. Exhaustion is proven by the tender, the consents and the signed Limited Release, with the check copy to follow, and it belongs on page one of each. Check every figure against the audit, answer the gap and “degenerative” with the MRI, and hand in two QC'd drafts routed to Atty. Thorne.
task.ask: Why does Cardinal State's demand say excess?

check.say: Check your two packages before you route them. Are they truly two, each complete on its own? Cardinal State gets the whole file, not a cross-reference to Harbor Point's. Is Relative UM framed as excess, claimed for damages above $30,000? Is exhaustion on page one of each: the 08/12 tender, Keystone's 03/20 Dec Page, Smith's 08/10 affidavit, the consents, the 08/28 release, and a task for the check copy? Are the 03/02 and 03/09 coverage letters in? Does your gap section answer “degenerative” with the radiologist's own words, “no significant degenerative change at the adjacent levels”? If it doesn't, you haven't learned from the BI round. Is there a two-page treatment summary instead of a record dump? And is the response deadline a marked blank for Atty. Thorne, with nothing served?
check.ask: Does Dr. Reyes's MMI note carry an impairment rating, and if not, what do you ask Atty. Thorne?

questions.say: This is your Learning Check for the demand module. The questions are on the screen, and your answers come from this file, in your own words, typed right under each question. State the BI demand's terms, how it was served and the date its window closed, and show me how you counted. Name the five elements, with this file's example of each, and tell me who decides bad faith. Then answer Keystone's degenerative and gap arguments with the documents, and say where each goes in the package. When you reach the pressure questions, I want the process, not the law. Use the file's own dates and figures, not general rules.
questions.ask: Before you start, what does a UM carrier's consent actually protect?

summary.say: Now the Self-Summary. In your own words, write what you learned serving John Doe's demands, the principles that make a demand hold, not the clicks. Then your strategy: with both UM drafts on Atty. Thorne's desk on 08/31/2026, what's your next action, and why that one? And name the one thing you're least confident about. Before anyone writes, look at the scenario on screen. Keystone's draft release arrives 08/14/2026 releasing all other insurers, Harbor Point hasn't answered the consent request, and Atty. Thorne is out until Monday. Let's talk it through together first.
summary.ask: With Atty. Thorne out until Monday, what must not happen to Keystone's release before he's back?

scale.say: Last step, the Skill Scale. Rate yourself 1 to 5 on each competency, from docketing a Time-Limited Demand from receipt all the way to holding the UPL boundary on terms, extensions and releases. Be honest with yourself. I'm going to compare your rating with your score, and a 5 on a block scored at 60 is a conversation, just like a 2 on a block you aced. And remember, UPL is a gate. A strong score doesn't survive an ethics breach. When you're done, submit it for review.
scale.ask: Where's the widest gap between how you rated yourself and how you actually scored?

why.say: Let's start with the question Dana Whitfield is going to ask, not the one we'd like her to ask: “Why did he wait two weeks?” Answer me from documents only. No adjectives. Here's the reality of this file. Keystone won't argue the crash. Robert Smith was cited, and the doorbell camera caught him. So it'll argue the 14-Day Gap, it'll call the MRI degenerative, and it'll stall toward 08/21/2026. A Case Manager who has mapped both attacks, and the documents that answer them, before the first call turns every stall into a record. That's what today is about.
why.ask: “Why did he wait two weeks?” Which documents answer her, with no adjectives?

theory.say: In personal injury, the demand letter is your opening move, and adjusters protect the carrier by undervaluing claims. So negotiation is prepared, never improvised. Four ideas carry it. The pitch: a demand that reads like a template gets treated like one, while a tailored presentation earns a real evaluation. Value drivers: the few facts that would scare a jury, because they create the carrier's risk, so every call leads with them. Anticipate the response: name your top two weaknesses before the adjuster does, and have the documents in hand. And the professional pause. After a low number, stay quiet. Silence shifts the burden back, and the adjuster has to justify the figure with data.
theory.ask: Who here has used a professional pause on a call, and how long could you hold the silence?

frame.say: Here's the battle map, four steps, built before any phone rings. Step one, create a Net Sheet. Total the liens, costs and attorney's fee, because below that line the client receives $0. Step two, identify the value drivers, three facts that would scare a jury, and every call leads with them. Step three, anticipate the adjuster's response: name your top two weaknesses and the documents that justify them. Step four, prepare the rebuttal so it's ready before they ever bring it up. On John Doe's file, the weaknesses aren't a mystery. It's the gap and the degenerative MRI, every single time.
frame.ask: On John Doe's file, which three facts would scare a jury the most?

rules.say: These are the rules, and where your authority ends. The net floor is liens plus costs plus fee. $6,485.00 plus $486.75 is $6,971.75, and grossing that up for the one-third fee gives $10,457.63, which is above Keystone's whole $10,000 limit. Every layer matters. Lead with the value drivers: Smith on video with an independent witness, the C5-C6 herniation and injection, residual right-arm paresthesia at MMI. Anchor on $16,401.40 in total Specials, never PIP's $5,000. Soft lead on the call, restate the demand and its 08/21/2026 deadline, then pause and ask for her data. Name every stall. Keystone's $3,500 is a counteroffer, logged in her exact words, and whether it ended the demand is Atty. Thorne's call. You present, ask, restate and relay. You never counter, move the number or the deadline, or tell John Doe what an offer's worth.
rules.ask: If this file settled for Keystone's full $10,000 and nothing else, what would John Doe net?

model.say: And the answer to that question, on unreduced liens, is $0. This is the battle map for Keystone, finished before the phone rings. Station one is the net floor, $10,457.63 gross, with that red note reminding you Keystone's limit is only $10,000. Station two holds the value drivers. Station three is their top two attacks in red, the 14-day gap and the “degenerative” MRI. And station four answers each one with a source: the EMS report and the 06/19/2026 Causation Letter for the gap, and the Summit MRI of 03/13/2026 for degenerative. Up in the corner, the demand expires 08/21/2026. Every attack on this file has a document waiting for it before she dials.
model.ask: If she opens with the gap, which card on station four do you read from first?

job.say: Here's how it plays out on the job. Keystone receives the demand on 07/22/2026, and that's your trigger to build the battle map and compute the net floor on the Net Sheet: $10,457.63 gross on unreduced liens, with every attack matched to a dated document in Case Notes. When the adjuster calls with an offer, you soft-lead, pause, ask for her data and restate the approved demand. You'll practice exactly that in the Call Simulator against Dana Whitfield. No counter, terms and deadline unchanged. When the call ends, log the offer and her exact words in the Communications Log and report to Atty. Thorne that day. And if she stalls with “waiting on authority,” you name it and send a same-day email citing 08/21/2026. No open-ended callbacks.

dodont.say: Let's play Three Clues, One Rule. I'll reveal three clues, you call Do or Don't, and you name the rule. Here's the territory. Making the adjuster justify her number with data, and using silence after a low offer. Staying firm, factual and professional, because an angry call is a gift to the carrier. Personalizing every answer to John Doe's record. And the traps: softening the demand to seem reasonable, negotiating without knowing the net floor, anchoring on PIP's $5,000, Specials that don't reconcile to the ledger, accepting “I'll get back to you.” One thing I'll be listening for: nobody apologizes for the gap. It's already explained, by the EMS report, the call-outs, the receipt, the numbness and the Causation Letter. Keep your tone flat and factual.
dodont.ask: What's the difference between holding the demand and softening it to seem reasonable?

why.say: I've got Harbor Point's 03/02/2026 letter up, and I want you to find the sentence in it that's worth $10,000 to John Doe. Give it a second. It's the add-on clause. On a reduction policy, Keystone's $10,000 would have come straight off the top of the $20,000. Once Keystone tenders, the money that makes John Doe whole sits with two first-party carriers that insure him, and both of them will argue against him. We reach $40,000 by proving the gap above each layer, closing every reduction in writing first, and papering every single move.
why.ask: Without that add-on sentence, what would Harbor Point's $20,000 have shrunk to?

theory.say: A UM settlement is won on paper. The package shows the other driver's fault, and it shows that damages exceed what's been collected. Compare a weak file with a legal trap. Raw charts and a casual letter carry no risk for the carrier, while a coded summary on a clock raises it. Sort documents by function, coverage, liability and damages, and let the diagnostics and a causation narrative answer any pre-existing-condition defense. You'll hear about bracketing, paired ranges that build a bridge across a gap and then close in the middle, but Atty. Thorne makes every move there. And in no-fault states, PIP set-off generally bars double recovery: value minus PIP paid is what the defendant still owes.
theory.ask: Has anyone worked a no-fault file, and how did PIP change the ask?

frame.say: Here's what goes inside a UM demand packet, in four groups. Evidence of liability: the Police Report, property-damage photos, witness statements, any dashcam or surveillance footage. On our file, that's the citation, Ruth Calloway and the doorbell video. Economic damages: itemized Medical Bills, complete records, lost-wage verification and future medical estimates. Non-economic damages: the demand letter, the client's impact statement and photos of injuries. And proof of exhaustion, which UM carriers look for first: the signed Limited Release, the check copy, the at-fault Dec Page and the consent to settle. Get that last group wrong and the rest barely matters.
frame.ask: Which of the four groups was still incomplete on John Doe's file on 08/31/2026?

rules.say: Here are the rules, and where you stop. UM pays the gap: damages as Atty. Thorne values them, minus the BI, up to its limit. Cardinal State's file has to show damages above $30,000. Check the offset rule first; Harbor Point's 03/02/2026 letter answers the limit half of “BI already compensated him,” and the medical proof answers the damages half. Both carriers turn adversarial at evaluation, so the first offer is rarely the last. Bracketing is Atty. Thorne's tool alone. When a carrier offers limits, confirm coverage, release scope, liens, payee and check date without accepting, and report that day. Never accept verbally under pressure. Riverton's PIP is add-on, and here it creates no lien and no UM cut. You assemble, log, relay and paper John Doe's decision. You never accept, reject, counter, explain offset language to him, or accuse a carrier of bad faith.
rules.ask: Harbor Point insures Kevin Alvarez's car. Why does it owe John Doe anything, and why will it still fight him?

model.say: This slide shows what could shrink the gross, and where this file actually stands. Three rungs build left to right: BI at $10,000, tendered 08/12, then Host UM at $20,000, then Relative UM at $10,000, with the running total going from $10,000 to $30,000 to $40,000 gross. Under the Host UM rung you'll see three reductions struck through in red: a BI offset, PIP non-duplication and a PIP lien. None of them apply, and one document knocks out all three, Harbor Point's letter of 03/02/2026. Off to the side sits a reminder that this PIP is add-on, so there's no set-off. Along the bottom is what we confirm before anything's accepted: scope, release, liens, payee and check date, then a confirming email.
model.ask: How does a single 03/02/2026 letter knock out all three of those red chips?

job.say: Let's run it on the calendar. On 09/14/2026, Harbor Point's offer comes in. You log the offer and its stated reasons in the Negotiation Log on the Insurance tab and report it to Atty. Thorne that day. Because the offer cites the BI payment and the gap, you assemble a counter-package for his approval: the 03/02/2026 letter, the MRI read, the Causation Letter, the MMI residuals and future care. He approves, and it goes out 09/16. When a carrier offers limits, you confirm the terms without accepting and draft the acceptance email, which goes only after John Doe's decision is logged and Atty. Thorne approves. And when each UM check arrives, you confirm its release is signed and deposit it to trust that day, 10/05 and 10/13/2026.

dodont.say: Three Clues, One Rule again. I reveal three clues, you call Do or Don't, then name the rule. In play this time: hunting down every stacking and resident-relative policy, because that's why this file reaches $40,000. Getting offset and reimbursement status in writing, the way Harbor Point's 03/02/2026 letter does. Setting John Doe's expectations on the UM timeline without ever promising him a limit. And the traps: taking the first offer because it's his own coverage, promising limits before the offset rule is checked, a bracket move with nothing back from the carrier, a verbal deal with no confirming email, finding a lien after disbursement. And remember, anyone who writes the words “bad faith” to an adjuster has crossed the line. That's Atty. Thorne's conclusion to draw.
dodont.ask: Harbor Point offered $8,000 on 09/14. What does that tell you about first-party carriers being friendly?

Her reasons: John Doe waited two weeks before seeking any treatment, and the MRI findings are degenerative in nature. She's calling this afternoon. Keep the facts in front of you. Keystone received the $10,000 Time-Limited Demand on 07/22, and acceptance runs to 08/21/2026. Atty. Thorne's written authority says restate the Limits Demand and the deadline, present the record, no counter, and report any offer to him the same day. Then your strategy: if a carrier's offer landed today, what's your next action, and why is it the right one rather than a counter? Then the one thing you're least confident about. Before anyone writes, here's a pressure question out loud. The offer dies at 5:00 p.m. and Atty. Thorne is unreachable. Turn to your neighbor, talk it through for a minute, and then write. scale.say: Okay, the Skill Scale. Give yourself a 1 to 5 on each of the six competencies, from building the battle map and net floor through to holding the authority line, where every number and decision runs through Atty. Thorne. I'll set your self-rating next to your score, and if they're far apart in either direction, we'll talk about it. That's not a penalty, it's coaching. Just keep in mind that UPL is a gate, so a strong score can't rescue an ethics breach. Submit it for review when you're finished.

why.say: Quick question to start. How many liens are on John Doe's $40,000? Most of you will say two. The right answer is two asserted and five checked, each one recorded with its source. Here's why that matters. That $40,000 isn't John Doe's until every claim on it is found, classified and resolved in writing. And liens aren't created equal. A statutory lien bends to a formula, a Health Plan's reimbursement right bends to a doctrine, and a provider's balance bends to a negotiation. Classify one wrong and you either overpay it or freeze the disbursement. Neither is okay with me.
why.ask: How many liens are on John Doe's $40,000, counting the ones we checked and found absent?

theory.say: The legal backing behind a lien decides how negotiable it is. At the easy end, medical provider liens. Providers treating on an LOP are highly negotiable, and they'll often take a reduction to get paid now. Health insurance subrogation, a private plan's reimbursement right, is moderate, shaped by the made-whole and common-fund doctrines. Medicare and Medicaid are government payers bound by strict federal or state formulas, so they're low negotiability and slow to process. And ERISA plans, self-funded employer plans governed by federal law, are very low, notoriously hard to reduce. Keep that ladder in your head, because it tells you where your leverage lives before you pick up the phone.
theory.ask: Which of these lien types have you dealt with, and which one gave you the hardest time?

frame.say: This chart puts the common lien types side by side, so you can see who they are and how far they'll bend. Medical providers, doctors or hospitals treating on a Letter of Protection, sit high; they often take a reduction to get paid now. Health insurance, private insurers seeking subrogation, sits moderate, subject to made whole or common fund. Medicare and Medicaid, the government-funded programs, sit low, with strict formulas and slow processing. ERISA plans, self-funded employer Health Plans, sit very low, governed by federal law and notoriously hard to reduce. On John Doe's file, Riverton Spine & Rehab is our LOP provider, and Peach State is a fully insured Health Plan, not ERISA.
frame.ask: Where do Riverton Spine & Rehab and Peach State land on this chart, and why?

rules.say: Here are the rules, and where your role stops. Statutory liens, like Medicare, Medicaid, a hospital lien or workers' comp, arise by law and bend least; contractual claims rest on an agreement. Inventory every claimant, absent ones included. Two liens are asserted, Peach State and Riverton Spine & Rehab, and every “none” gets its source. Not every payer is a lienholder: Harbor Point's PIP has no reimbursement right, and Crescent Pain & Spine can't balance-bill. Peach State is fully insured, and what follows is Atty. Thorne's call. He asked for the one-third common-fund share, so $1,860.00 minus $620.00 is $1,240.00. Made whole, comparative fault and quantum meruit are doctrines you can name, never choose. You classify, gather, audit and draft. You never compromise a lien without his authority, or tell John Doe a lien is invalid.
rules.ask: Peach State paid $1,860.00 on a $3,400.00 injection. Who can come after John Doe for the other $1,540.00?

model.say: Nobody can, by the way, because Crescent took the contract rate. Now, this slide classifies every claim on John Doe's $40,000. The ladder runs from most negotiable at the top, the provider LOP, through fully insured Health Plans and workers' comp, down to Medicare and Medicaid, with ERISA self-funded at the bottom. Only two bars are solid: Riverton Spine & Rehab at $6,290.00 and Peach State at $1,860.00. Every other bar is hollow, with a green check saying none, verified. There's an outlined prior-attorney bar tagged quantum meruit, and three doctrine cards, common fund, made whole and comparative fault, with that last one greyed out. And the warning along the bottom: unclassified means overpaid or frozen.
model.ask: Why is the comparative fault card greyed out on John Doe's file?

job.say: Let's put it on the job. When the gross reaches $40,000.00 on 10/06/2026, you run the final inventory in the Lien Tracker, re-verifying the Day 2 register, asserted and absent, and classifying each claim as statutory or contractual. Two stay open; Medicare, Medicaid, hospital, workers' comp, prior attorney and PIP each get “none” with a source. Once the Health Plan lien is classified, you get the plan documents and escalate the funding status to Atty. Thorne. Fully insured goes on file, and the governing-law call is recorded as his. When he picks the reduction basis, you draft the request naming the doctrine and showing $1,860.00 minus $620.00 equals $1,240.00, held for his approval. And for the prior-attorney question, ask John Doe, check intake, and log “no prior attorney, verified” with its date.

dodont.say: Here comes Three Clues, One Rule. I reveal three clues, you call Do or Don't, then name the rule. The rules in play: work the most negotiable lien first to build momentum, but resolve every one in writing before disbursement. Record a verified “none” the way you'd record a lien, with its source and date. Name the doctrine and show the math in every Reduction Request. And the traps: treating an ERISA plan like a provider LOP, asking for a courtesy discount with no legal basis, paying a prior attorney a percentage he's no longer owed. One heads-up. Someone will ask whether riding in Kevin Alvarez's carpool makes this workers' comp. That's a coverage question for Atty. Thorne. We record that no claim was filed and no lien asserted.
dodont.ask: With no prior attorney on this file, why does quantum meruit still get a line in the Lien Tracker?

why.say: Look at this table. It's what would have happened with only Keystone's $10,000 BI, and I've covered the last row. What does John Doe take home? Here it is: $0.00. That's why this lesson exists. Half the job is getting money from the carriers. The other half is keeping it from the lienholders, because every dollar a lien gives up lands in John Doe's net. And what moves a provider isn't a plea for a favor. It's an honest audit and the pro-rata math, laid out so plainly the provider can check it themselves.
why.ask: Before I uncover that last row, what do you think John Doe takes home on BI alone?

map.say: Here's the road to reducing the liens. You start by auditing the bill line by line against the records, and corrections come before any reduction. Then you run the pro rata math, from the fraction, not a rounded percentage. Then you ask with authority: Atty. Thorne's written request and his target, never a stock number. Nothing gets paid without a Payoff Letter that says full and final, in writing. And the day a reduction is confirmed, you update the ledger and show John Doe what it saved him.

theory.say: Before you ever ask for a discount, make sure the bill is accurate. An error earns a demand for correction, not a favor. Watch for upcoding, which is billing a higher service level than the records support, like a Level 5 for a Level 3, and the record decides. Watch for unbundling, one service split into separately billed parts to inflate the total. Then pro-rata distribution: when a short fund can't pay everyone, equal-priority liens split it in proportion, each lien's amount over all the liens, times what's left. And the common fund doctrine says the lienholder shouldn't ride free on the work and costs that created the fund it's repaid from.
theory.ask: Have you ever caught a billing error that the provider fixed without an argument?

frame.say: Here's the path from the bill to the payoff. Cross-reference first, records against bill, so a Level 3 visit billed as Level 5 gets corrected, not discounted. Hunt for duplicate charges, especially overlapping dates between hospital stays and individual physician groups. Then leverage the common fund. In many states a lienholder reduces by its share of fees and costs, and Atty. Thorne makes that argument. Finally, the Payoff Letter. Never pay without a signed letter saying it's full and final satisfaction of the lien. On John Doe's file, the duplicate check has already found something on Riverton's ledger.
frame.ask: What did the duplicate check find on Riverton Spine & Rehab's ledger?

rules.say: Here are the rules, and your line. Audit before you ask: corrections first, reductions second. Riverton billed 34 lines at $185.00, $6,290.00, but the records show 33 visits and a duplicate on 05/04/2026, so you negotiate from $6,105.00. Match each code to that day's note; nothing may fall between 04/02 and 04/21/2026. With only the BI, $6,179.92 would split pro rata, Peach State $1,772.50 and Riverton $4,407.42, and John Doe nets nothing. But on Track A the fund covers both liens, so argue true facts only. Never say a provider would take only a share or that the client will refuse the settlement. Common fund is Atty. Thorne's argument. Send his approved request, call with his target, and remember, no Payoff Letter means no payment. You never offer or accept outside his authority.
rules.ask: Riverton billed $6,290.00. What number do you negotiate from?

model.say: Here's the pro-rata illustration, on BI alone. That long bar is the $6,179.92 left after fee and costs, split 28.68% to Peach State, which is $1,772.50, and 71.32% to Riverton Spine & Rehab, which is $4,407.42. Underneath, you can see $6,485.00 of liens hanging off the end in red hatching, and that little red card on the right says it all: John Doe nets $0.00. Along the bottom is the order of work. Audit, correct, calculate, ask with authority, confirm in writing, and then the Net Sheet gets updated. The math is the leverage, and the audit always comes before the ask.
model.ask: Why do we compute each share from the fraction instead of the rounded percentage?

job.say: On the job, it runs in three beats. When the provider's Final Ledger arrives, you audit each line against the visit records you requested, and you ask in writing for any error to be corrected. On John Doe's file, that's 33 visits matched, the 05/04/2026 duplicate removed, and $6,105.00 in the Lien Tracker. With the audited balance confirmed, you draft the Reduction Request with the math and get Atty. Thorne's written authority, escalated through CMS. That authority is logged before the request goes out or any call is made. And when a reduction is agreed, you get the signed Payoff Letter, update the Lien Tracker and the Net Sheet, and recompute the net that same day.

dodont.say: Let's play Three Clues, One Rule. Three clues come up, you call Do or Don't, and you name the rule. In play: corrections first, reductions second. Being transparent with John Doe about the savings, so he sees his net rising. Getting every reduction in writing before disbursement. And the traps: a percentage off an inflated bill, a verbal reduction with nothing in writing, paying from a statement instead of the final payoff figure. Now, a warning about an old script you may hear: “reduce or the client refuses the settlement.” That's a threat, and here it's false. After fee and costs, $26,179.92 remains against $6,485.00 of liens. Use true facts instead: a coverage-capped recovery, the audited balance, a certain payment now.
dodont.ask: How would you rewrite “reduce or the client refuses the settlement” using only true facts?

Peach State Health Plan asserts its reimbursement right of $1,860.00, paid for the 05/15/2026 epidural injection at Crescent Pain & Spine, and asks us to confirm its claim will be protected from the proceeds. On the left is the Lien Tracker with one live row, Peach State going from $1,860.00 to $1,240.00, with the math underneath: $1,860.00 times one-third is $620.00. Below it are the hollow rows, each stamped none, verified, with its source: BCRC, Medicaid verified, Harbor Point's 03/02/2026 letter, intake. On the right is the draft Reduction Request for Atty. Thorne's signature, with a red hold tag across the corner. And between them, an escalation to Atty. Elijah Thorne on governing law and doctrine. The point of the picture is the division of labor. check.say: Before you log it, check yourself. Is the plan ledger matched to the one accident-related charge, the 05/15/2026 injection, $3,400.00 billed and $1,860.00 paid? The lien is what the plan paid, not what was billed. Is Crescent's $1,540.00 write-off recorded as not owed? Is the lien classified contractual, with fully insured status from the plan documents and the governing law recorded as Atty. Thorne's call? Is the common-fund math shown, citing the MRI and the 06/19/2026 Causation Letter? Are the absences complete, Medicare, Medicaid, hospital, workers' comp and prior attorney, each with date and source, and PIP recorded as not a lien? And did you log $1,240.00 as final only with Peach State's written confirmation and Atty. Thorne's approval attached? That's where people trip.
check.ask: Who checked Summit Imaging, which asked for an LOP on 03/11/2026?

why.say: Here's a question to start. Riverton Spine & Rehab has agreed to take less. What has to be in the file before a dollar goes out? Most people say the agreement. It's the signed Payoff Letter. A reduction is won on paper first and on the phone second. The lienholder needs to see the audited balance, the recovery, the fee and costs, and the other liens, so it can see why taking less is fair. And it needs a letter it can sign that closes the bill for good. Skip the paper and you either leave money on the table or reopen a bill you thought was closed.
why.ask: What goes to the lienholder before you ever pick up the phone?

rules.say: Four rules carry this. First, you negotiate from the audited balance, never the billed one: Riverton at $4,625.00, Peach State at $1,860.00, $6,485.00 in all. Second, the written Reduction Request goes first, with Atty. Thorne's written authority already on file. Third, on the call you make his ask and nothing outside it, and you log the name, the date and every figure. A counter outside his authority goes back to him the same day. Fourth, no Payoff Letter, no payment, and the letter says full and final, with no balance billing or collections. Then you update the Lien Tracker and the Net Sheet that day.

job.say: Here's the job, start to finish. When the audited balance is confirmed, you draft the Reduction Request with the math and get Atty. Thorne's written authority before it goes. When the lienholder responds, you call with the authorized ask and log who you spoke to, when, and every figure. And when the reduction is agreed, you get the signed Payoff Letter, then update the Lien Tracker and the Net Sheet so John Doe can see his net change the same day.

Thorne has set a target for Riverton in writing, and the Reduction Request is yours to draft. We're running this one live. Thorne's approval, and send it once he approves. Next comes the follow-up call in the Call Simulator with Tammy Greer, the billing manager. Did you request the written correction for the 05/04/2026 duplicate before any reduction, taking $6,290.00 down to $6,105.00? No lines between 04/02 and 04/21/2026? questions.say: This is the Lien Reduction Verification. Answer from the file, in your own words, typed under each question. First, classify each claim on John Doe's $40,000, that's Peach State, Riverton Spine & Rehab, PIP, Medicare and Medicaid, and a prior attorney, as statutory, contractual or none, and rank the liens by reducibility. scale.say: Now the Skill Scale for this module. Rate yourself 1 to 5 on each skill, from classifying liens as statutory or contractual right through to holding the authority line in lien negotiation. I'll compare each rating with your score. If you gave yourself a 5 and scored 60, or a 2 and aced it, we'll sit down and talk about why. And remember, UPL is a gate. No score survives an ethics breach. Submit when you're ready.

why.say: Let me write two numbers on the board: $6,179.92 against $6,485.00. That's the BI stream alone. What would John Doe have taken home? Nothing at all. Now here's what he actually nets: $21,469.92. The difference is why the Net Sheet matters. His $40,000 came from three carriers in two streams, and it goes out as five checks. The Net Sheet shows where every dollar came from and where it's going before a cent leaves trust. If you can't trace a dollar on the sheet, it doesn't move.
why.ask: What turned $0.00 into $21,469.92 on this file?

theory.say: The Net Sheet is your tool for transparency and case control. Think of it in two streams. The third-party BI stream comes from the at-fault driver's carrier, and exhausting its limit is usually a legal prerequisite to first-party UM. The first-party UM stream comes from the client's own policy or a resident relative's, and it only triggers once BI is exhausted or the driver is uninsured. Then there's the double-dipping trap. Carriers audit files closely, so tracing every dollar's source keeps liens paid correctly without cross-contaminating funds. And the final aggregate net puts both streams side by side, so the client sees what the coverages and the negotiation added.
theory.ask: Have you seen money double-counted on a settlement before, and how was it caught?

frame.say: Here are the two streams on John Doe's Net Sheet. Stream one is third-party BI, the at-fault driver's insurance company. You exhaust its limit first, because that's usually a legal prerequisite, and here it's Keystone, $10,000. Stream two is first-party UM or UIM, a host vehicle's or resident relative's policy that triggers only once BI is exhausted or the tortfeasor is uninsured. On our file that's $20,000 from Harbor Point plus $10,000 from Cardinal State. Keep them in separate columns from the first entry to the last, and you'll never have to untangle them later.
frame.ask: Why did Stream 2 only open after Keystone paid its full $10,000?

rules.say: Here are the rules, and where your role stops. One Net Sheet, two tabs. The Recovery Ledger carries money in and every deduction, and the Lien Tracker proves each lien figure. Neither is final until they tie out. Keep the streams apart, BI $10,000.00 and UM $30,000.00. PIP's $5,000.00 is a payment source on the Lien Tracker, never recovery. Price the fee per stream at 33⅓% pre-suit: $3,333.33 plus $10,000.00 is $13,333.33. Every cost needs a receipt, $486.75 in all, split 25% and 75%, $121.69 and $365.06. Reduce liens globally, then allocate pro rata. Run the net both ways: $5,367.48 plus $16,102.44 is $21,469.92. Flag future ESIs of $3,400 to $6,800 for Atty. Thorne. You build and explain the arithmetic. You never tell John Doe whether the net is enough.
rules.ask: Why does Harbor Point's PIP appear on the Lien Tracker but not in the gross?

Down the rows you've got the gross, the 33⅓% fee, costs, Peach State and Riverton Spine & Rehab, closing on that heavy orange net row: $21,469.92, which is $5,367.48 plus $16,102.44. See those thin orange lines running from each lien row back to the Lien Tracker tab? They read proved by Payoff Letter. And in the corner, the reminder that BI alone meant $0.00 to John Doe. job.say: On the job, the Net Sheet builds as the file moves. Each settlement check that arrives gets posted to its stream on the Recovery Ledger, with carrier and check reference: BI $10,000.00, UM $20,000.00 plus $10,000.00, $40,000.00 total. Each cost gets its receipt attached and is posted once; five receipts make $486.75, and nothing is charged to both streams in full. When a lien reduction is accepted, the Lien Tracker gets the asserted, audited and reduced figures and the Payoff Letter: Peach State $1,240.00, Riverton Spine & Rehab $3,470.00, letters dated. And once both tabs are complete, you tie the Net Sheet to the Trust Ledger, net $21,469.92 on both, and route it to Atty. Thorne before John Doe ever sees it.

dodont.say: Time for Three Clues, One Rule. I reveal three clues, you call Do or Don't, then name the rule. The rules this time: one Net Sheet, two clearly separated streams. Every reduction carries its reason, an audit finding like the 05/04/2026 duplicate or a named basis like the one-third procurement-cost reduction. Show the streams side by side so John Doe sees what the work produced, from Keystone's $3,500 offer to its $10,000, and then $30,000 more from UM. And the traps: BI and UM mixed on one line, one cost charged to both streams, a cost with no receipt or a lien with no Payoff Letter. Watch your rounding too. BI carries $121.69 of the costs, and UM takes the remainder, $365.06.
dodont.ask: Why do we compute the UM share as the remainder instead of rounding it on its own?

why.say: I've got a line from Keystone's 08/14 draft up here, struck through: “all other persons, firms, corporations and insurers.” What would that one line have cost John Doe if nobody had read it? $30,000. It would have released both UM carriers. That's the whole case for auditing every release. A settlement isn't over when a carrier says yes. It's over when the right release is signed, every check has cleared trust, every lien is paid off in writing, and the ledger reads $0.00. Until then, the work isn't done.
why.ask: When any release lands on your desk, what's the first thing you read for?

map.say: Here's the road from a signed deal to a ledger at zero. First, audit the release line by line: who's released, which claims, and what John Doe promises. Second, both UM consents come in before the BI release is signed. Third, the Settlement Statement shows him how $40,000.00 becomes his net. Fourth, trust: each check goes to IOLTA the same day its release is signed, and nothing is paid against uncleared funds. And fifth, disbursement: Payoff Letters, Atty. Thorne's signature, and a ledger that reads $0.00.

theory.say: Four documents close a case, and you need to know what each one does. The Release of All Claims is the exit document that ends the right to sue, and its scope decides which claims and carriers survive. The Settlement Disclosure Statement is the truth document: gross to net, and a clear statement that full and final means there's no coming back for more. A Satisfaction of Lien is the provider's signed letter that its lien is paid, which prevents collections against the client later. And where suit was filed, a Dismissal With Prejudice tells the court it's over, and with prejudice means it can't be refiled. After that, disbursement moves money only through verification, documentation, authorization and reconciliation.
theory.ask: Which of these four documents has John Doe's file not needed, and why?

frame.say: Here's the disbursement workflow, four stages, and each one protects accuracy, compliance and the client against fraud. Verification first: you review the Ready for Payment files and confirm every condition precedent is met. Then documentation: you collect the invoices and receipts and make sure each one is legible and matches the claim. Then authorization: Atty. Thorne approves and signs, and the packet goes to accounting. You never sign it. And finally reconciliation: you confirm receipt of the funds and update the case file to show Paid. On John Doe's file, all four stages land between 10/20 and 10/22/2026.
frame.ask: Which condition precedent on John Doe's file was the last to close before 10/22?

rules.say: Here are the rules, and where you stop. Read every release line by line before John Doe sees it: who's released, which claims, what he promises. A BI release can't reach what's still open, like the Civic's property-damage claim with Keystone PD, and both UM consents come before it's signed. The indemnity clause binds John Doe to repay the carrier if a lienholder later pursues it, so every lien must be tracked and paid off in writing. Harbor Point's release must not reach Cardinal State. The Settlement Statement shows $40,000.00 becoming $21,469.92. Log each check on arrival, deposit to IOLTA once its release is signed, and never disburse before funds clear on 10/20. No suit was filed here, so no dismissal. You audit, flag, prepare and verify. Atty. Thorne explains, approves and signs.
rules.ask: Keystone's check is in. Why can't we pay Riverton Spine & Rehab today?

model.say: This is John Doe's money path, and no gate opens before the one to its left has closed. Gate one, the releases signed, 08/28 plus the UM releases. Gate two, the checks into IOLTA on 09/04, 10/05 and 10/13. Gate three, funds clear on 10/20. Gate four, the statement is signed on 10/21. Gate five, Atty. Thorne signs on 10/22. Gate six, reconciled to $0.00. Above gate one is that struck-through line again, with minus $30,000 beside it, and underneath, the Trust Ledger steps down from $40,000.00 to $0.00. So here's your answer: we can't pay Riverton until funds clear, the statement is signed, the Payoff Letter is in hand and Atty. Thorne signs.

job.say: Here's how it runs on the job. When a settlement is agreed or tendered, request the payee's W-9 the same day and send it back with the signed release, so accounting never holds the check. When a carrier's draft release arrives, audit the parties, claims, indemnity, Medicare and confidentiality terms in the release audit, and route a redline memo; every over-broad line gets quoted and flagged before John Doe sees it. When a check arrives, confirm its release is signed, deposit it to IOLTA that day and log the clearance date: 09/04, 10/05 and 10/13, $40,000.00, all cleared by 10/20. And if a suit is pending, which isn't Track A, you prepare the stipulation of dismissal with prejudice, docket it and confirm the court entry.

dodont.say: Let's play Three Clues, One Rule. Three clues, you call Do or Don't, then name the rule. In play: matching each document to its signer, the release to John Doe, the Payoff Letter to the lienholder, the W-9 to the payee, a dismissal to the attorneys. Secure e-signature or an in-person signing, with a current notary stamp and ID matching “John Doe” exactly. The Kickback Protocol: say exactly what's missing and give a deadline. Cross-referencing invoice numbers, which is how we caught the 05/04/2026 duplicate. And the traps: a General Release that wipes out UM or the property-damage claim, checks against uncleared funds, payment instructions taken from an email without a phone check. And that indemnity clause? Not boilerplate. It's John Doe's promise that every lien gets paid.
dodont.ask: What makes it safe for John Doe to sign that indemnity promise?

That joins Keystone's check, received 09/04, and Harbor Point's, 10/05, each deposited only after its release was signed. Trust has received $40,000.00. Peach State accepted $1,240.00 on 10/09 and Riverton Spine & Rehab accepted $3,470.00 on 10/12, both in writing. Costs stand at $486.75. Why isn't PIP's $5,000.00 being paid back, and why isn't Crescent's write-off owed? Add either to the payables and you've paid John Doe's money away.

On the Recovery Ledger, post each check by carrier and stream, the 33⅓% fee per stream, the five receipted costs, and costs and liens split 25% and 75%, down to the net per stream and in total. On the Lien Tracker, list every provider and payer with charges, payments, adjustments and balance owed, then each lien's asserted, audited and reduced figure, the basis of each reduction and its payoff-letter status. Tie both tabs to the Trust Ledger. You'll hand in a two-tab Net Sheet reaching $21,469.92 down both streams and across the total, with every lien figure proved and routed to Atty. Thorne. And think hard about what you flag before John signs.

check.say: Check the arithmetic both ways before you log it. Gross: Keystone's $10,000.00 to Stream 1, Harbor Point and Cardinal State's $30,000.00 to Stream 2. Fee: $3,333.33 plus $10,000.00, $13,333.33. Costs: $486.75, split $121.69 and $365.06, charged once. Liens split 25% and 75%: Peach State $310.00 and $930.00, Riverton $867.50 and $2,602.50. Net: $5,367.48 plus $16,102.44 is $21,469.92, and $40,000.00 minus $18,530.08 lands in the same place. A one-cent drift means a stream got rounded on its own. Are the zero-balance lines kept off the payables, with their sources? Is each lien's payoff status recorded, none final on a phone call? And the judgment call: did you flag up to $6,800 in possible repeat injections to Atty. Thorne before John Doe signs?

questions.say: This is the Final Accounting Check. Your answers come from this file, in your own words, typed under each question. Question one is the keystone: take John Doe's $40,000.00 to his $21,469.92, stream by stream, with fee, costs and liens, and explain the 25% and 75% split. If you can't do that without notes, the Net Sheet isn't finished yet. Question two: name the four document sets needed before the file is archived, the item on this file for each, and the retention period. Question three: after the 10/22/2026 disbursement the Trust Ledger reads $0.00. Which records prove it, and what would a leftover balance tell you?

summary.say: Now the Self-Summary, in your own words: the principles behind the Net Sheet, the release audit and the Trust Ledger. Then your next action between the $0.00 ledger on 10/22/2026 and the 10/30/2026 closing memo, and why. Before anyone writes, a pressure question for the whole room. A $1,540.00 balance, the gap between $3,400.00 and $1,860.00 on Crescent's injection, turns up on John Doe's account. Look at Peach State's EOB before you answer. And keep the scenario on screen in mind. A deadline is never a reason to let John Doe sign a release that reaches $30,000 of UM coverage.
